title: Long-term effect of early-life stress from earthquake exposure on working memory in adulthood.
ehr_evidence: The subjects of present study were recruited from workers of Kailuan Mining Group in six coal reserve bases, two communities, and two related units.
summary: Observational study investigating the long-term effect of early-life earthquake exposure on working memory performance in adulthood.
key_findings: BVMT-R scores were markedly decreased in the infant exposure group compared with the no exposure group (P<0.05).
Subjects exposed prenatally in the second and third trimesters had significantly lower BVMT-R scores compared with the first trimester (P=0.035 for 2nd test, P=0.038 for total score).
HVLT-R scores did not show significant differences across the three groups (P>0.05).
Education level (OR=2.289, 95% CI=1.435–3.650, P<0.001) and earthquake exposure (OR=1.437, 95% CI=1.061–1.947, P=0.019) were independent risk factors for impaired visuospatial memory.
study_design: observational cross-sectional study based on historical birth dates and natural disaster exposure
population: 907 adult workers born in Tangshan, China between 1975 and 1978
exposure_domain: early-life stress from earthquake exposure (prenatal and infant periods)
limitations: confounding factors such as genetic background, adult life events, lifestyle, diet, alcohol, and drug abuse were difficult to quantify
no imaging or biological studies were performed to explore underlying mechanisms
